items.title: 12.1.2 Meaning of the Phrase "x approaches infinity"

blocks.text: Suppose a sequence \(x_{n} = 10^{n}\) assumes values as \(1, 10, 10^{2}, 10^{3}, \ldots, 10^{n}, \ldots\)

It is clear that the sequence \(x_{n}\) is becoming larger and larger as \(n\) increases and can be made as large as we please by taking \(n\) sufficiently large. This unending increase of the sequence \(x_{n}\) is symbolically written as "\(x_{n} \to \infty\)" and is read as "\(x_{n}\) approaches infinity" or "\(x_{n}\) tends to infinity" as \(n \to \infty\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The listed values start from \(1 = 10^{0}\), so here \(n\) runs through \(0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)
"As large as we please" means: name any big number, and from some term onwards every term is bigger. Example: to have \(x_{n} > 1{,}000{,}000 = 10^{6}\) we need \(10^{n} > 10^{6}\), i.e. \(n > 6\). So from the 7th power on, every term is bigger than a million; for a billion (\(10^{9}\)) take \(n > 9\).

blocks.caption: Our table (not in the book): the terms of x_n = 10^n grow without any bound as n grows.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Infinity (\(\infty\)) is not a number. You cannot add, subtract or substitute it like a number. \(x_{n} \to \infty\) is a short way of saying "\(x_{n}\) grows beyond every bound".
In the same way \(x \to -\infty\) means \(x\) becomes negative and larger and larger in size, e.g. \(-10, -100, -1000, \ldots\); you will meet it in 12.2.3.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Compare the two phrases: \(x_{n} \to 0\) (12.1.1) means the terms get as small (close to \(0\)) as we please; \(x_{n} \to \infty\) means the terms get as large as we please. In both cases \(n \to \infty\). Note also the link: if \(x_{n} = 10^{n} \to \infty\), then \(\frac{1}{x_{n}} = \frac{1}{10^{n}} \to 0\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(x_{n} = 10^{n}\) gives \(1, 10, 100, 1000, \ldots\): the terms increase without end.
2. They can be made larger than any number we choose by taking \(n\) large enough.
3. This is written \(x_{n} \to \infty\) as \(n \to \infty\) and read "\(x_{n}\) approaches (tends to) infinity".
4. \(\infty\) is a symbol for unbounded growth, not a real number.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Treating \(\infty\) as a number, e.g. writing \(10^{\infty}\) as an answer or \(\infty - \infty = 0\). These have no meaning.
2. Thinking that "getting larger" is enough. The terms \(1 - \frac{1}{n}\) get larger and larger but never pass \(1\); they do not tend to infinity. Tending to infinity needs growth beyond every bound.
